notes: Ruling slot 22 holds the Kuomintang (Chiang Kai-shek's party-state under martial law); the ROC Armed Forces (MD slot 22) move to slot 0 with their MD sprite. Coalition partner slot 13 = CIECD economic technocrats (Yen Chia-kan, K. T. Li, Sun Yun-suan). CDSP moved from MD slot 21 to 3 (democratic socialism); Blue Shirts veterans fill 21. Slot 7 = Chiang Ching-kuo's Leninist political warfare system. Young China Party kept in 20 as in MD. Slot 18 = WUFI (formed New Year 1970).

0.name: Zhonghua Minguo Guojun
0.text:
The Republic of China Armed Forces, some six hundred thousand strong, are the largest institution of the exiled state and the guarantor of the martial law in force since 1949. Their commanders are mostly mainland-born veterans of the civil war, and the Taiwan Garrison Command polices dissent on the island. Chiang Ching-kuo, defence minister from 1965 to 1969 and now vice-premier, controls their promotions.

Equipped and trained by the United States under the 1954 Mutual Defense Treaty, the armed forces are the most pro-American institution on the island. They garrison Kinmen and Matsu, plan for a counter-offensive against the mainland and see the Sino-Soviet split as an opportunity. Their leverage lies in their size, the military courts and Washington's aid.

1.name: CC Xi
1.text:
The CC Clique is the old organisational faction of the Kuomintang, built in the 1920s and 1930s by the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu around the party's organisation department and its first secret service. Eclipsed after 1950, when Chiang Kai-shek blamed it for the loss of the mainland and Chen Lifu went into exile in the United States, it survives in the Legislative Yuan and the party apparatus; Chen Lifu himself returned to Taiwan in 1969.

Its outlook is Confucian and conservative: party loyalty, filial piety, moral revival through the Chinese Cultural Renaissance Movement and implacable anti-communism within the American alliance. Its base is the mainland-born legislators elected in 1947–48, teachers and cultural bureaucrats who resent Chiang Ching-kuo's rising technocrats.

2.name: Dangwai
2.text:
Tangwai, 'outside the party', is the loose label for the independent politicians who contest the local and supplementary elections the Kuomintang permits. Its pioneers include the provincial assemblyman Kuo Yu-hsin; in December 1969 Huang Hsin-chieh won a seat in the supplementary Legislative Yuan election and Kang Ning-hsiang entered the Taipei City Council. It has no party, since new parties are banned under martial law, as Lei Chen's arrest in 1960 showed.

It demands an end to martial law, full elections for the national bodies frozen since 1948, freedom of the press and fair treatment for the island-born majority. Pro-American and anti-communist, it draws on Taiwanese small business, professionals and the provincial vote.

3.name: Zhongguo Minzhu Shehuidang
3.text:
The China Democratic Socialist Party was formed in 1946 by Carsun Chang (Zhang Junmai), the constitutional scholar who drafted much of the 1947 Constitution. It followed the government to Taiwan, where it survives as a legal but tiny 'friendly party' with subsidies and a handful of seats. Chang himself died in exile in California in February 1969, and the party is torn by factional quarrels over his succession.

It stands for parliamentary democracy and democratic socialism in the British manner: constitutional rule, civil liberties, social insurance and a mixed economy. It opposes communism and supports the American alliance, but its leverage is limited to its constitutional legitimacy and its occasional voice for reform inside the frozen parliament.

4.name: Taiwan Minzhu Zizhi Tongmeng
4.text:
Founded in Hong Kong in 1947 after the February 28 Incident by Taiwanese leftists led by Xie Xuehong, a co-founder of the prewar Taiwanese Communist Party, the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League is one of the eight democratic parties of the People's Republic. On Taiwan itself its underground networks were destroyed in the White Terror of the 1950s, and in Beijing Xie Xuehong has long since been purged.

The League calls for the liberation of Taiwan and its reunification with a socialist China, land to the tillers and punishment of Kuomintang repression. It looks to Beijing for leadership, and its leverage lies in the memory of 1947 and in Communist radio broadcasts across the strait.

5.name: Duli Taiwan Hui
5.text:
The Independent Taiwan Association was founded in Tokyo in 1967 by Su Beng, a Taiwanese Marxist who had worked with the Chinese Communists before breaking with them, and who runs a noodle shop in Ikebukuro to finance the cause. His 'Taiwan's 400-Year History' presents the Taiwanese as a nation forged by colonial exploitation. Its members are a few dozen students and workers in Japan.

The association combines socialism with Taiwanese independence and openly advocates underground cells and armed struggle against the Kuomintang regime. It rejects both Washington's patronage and Beijing's claims, and smuggles leaflets and activists onto the island through students and seamen.

6.name: Zhongguo Guomindang Geming Weiyuanhui
6.english: Revolutionary Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang
6.text:
The Revolutionary Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang, founded in Hong Kong in 1948 by Li Jishen and other Nationalists who went over to the Communists, claims to be the true heir of Sun Yat-sen's party. Based in Beijing under the elderly He Xiangning, it belongs to the Communist-led united front and appeals to former comrades on Taiwan through broadcasts and letters, although the Cultural Revolution has silenced it at home.

Nationalist and anti-American, it calls on Kuomintang officers and officials to 'return to the motherland', end the American military presence and reunify China in a patriotic alliance with Beijing. Its leverage lies in old personal networks, the homesickness of mainland-born veterans and the doubts sown by Washington's first overtures to Beijing.
6.wiki: Revolutionary Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang

7.name: Zong Zhengzhi Zuozhanbu
7.text:
The General Political Warfare Department is the political commissar system of the ROC armed forces, built by Chiang Ching-kuo in the 1950s on the Soviet model he learned during his years in Moscow. Its officers, trained at the Fu Hsing Kang College, sit in every unit and run indoctrination, counter-intelligence and loyalty checks. Its rising strongman is Wang Sheng, Chiang Ching-kuo's trusted protégé.

Leninist in method, it stands for party control of the gun, ideological mobilisation and absolute loyalty to the Chiang family. It distrusts American liberal influence and the Western press, and regards democracy as a security risk. Its leverage lies in control over officers' careers, surveillance files and the youth organisations around Chiang Ching-kuo.

8.name: Bosi Wenhua Hui
8.text:
The Persian Culture Circle gathers the small Iranian presence in Taipei, embassy staff, traders and students sent under the Imperial Iranian government's friendship with the Republic of China, together with Chinese Muslim scholars interested in Persian language and poetry. It meets in private homes and, on Shia holy days, in a side room of the Taipei Grand Mosque.

Its members follow the reformist Shia thinking heard in Tehran's religious lecture halls, which seeks to reconcile faith with science, social justice and national development. Loyal to the Shah's alliance with the West and staunchly anti-communist, the circle's influence lies in its links to Tehran and to the trade both countries are building.

9.name: Hey'at-e Hoseyni
9.text:
The Husayni Mourning Circle is a handful of Iranian students and seamen in Taiwan who gather each Muharram to mourn Imam Husayn and to read the declarations of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah and living in Najaf since 1965. Watched by informers of the Iranian embassy and SAVAK, they meet only behind closed doors in rented rooms.

They regard the Shah as a tyrant and an American puppet and call for an Islamic government guided by the clergy, the theme Khomeini is developing in Najaf. Hostile to Washington and Moscow alike, they have almost no foothold in Chinese society; their influence rests on networks of fellow students abroad and on pamphlets smuggled from Iraq.

10.name: Zhongguo Huijiao Xiehui
10.text:
The Chinese Muslim Association, re-established in Taipei by Hui officials and generals who followed the government into exile, represents the island's small Muslim community. It runs the Taipei Grand Mosque, inaugurated in 1960 with help from Muslim states, and organises the Hajj. Its long-time chairman, General Bai Chongxi, died in 1966, and its elders are veteran officers and diplomats.

It stands for a loyal, establishment Islam: patriotism, anti-communism and close ties with Saudi Arabia, Jordan and the other Muslim monarchies that still recognise the Republic of China. Its leverage lies in diplomacy: the former Qinghai warlord Ma Bufang, once ambassador to Saudi Arabia, lives in Jeddah and keeps the royal court's doors open to Taipei.

11.name: Xibei Huijun
11.text:
The veterans of the Ma family armies of Qinghai, Gansu and Ningxia, who fought the Communists in 1949 and in the guerrilla war that followed, form a close-knit brotherhood in Taiwan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey. Their patron is Ma Bufang in Jeddah, and they cultivate ties with the Uyghur exile leader Isa Yusuf Alptekin in Istanbul.

They see the struggle against communism as a holy war, call for the liberation of Xinjiang and the Muslim northwest, and dream of uniting the Muslims of Inner Asia in an Islamic polity under the sharia. Indifferent to Taipei's constitution, they rely on Muslim solidarity abroad, on Saudi money and on veterans' networks in the hills of Burma and Thailand.

12.name: Longgang Qingzhensi
12.text:
The congregation of the Longgang Mosque in Zhongli is formed by Yunnanese Hui soldiers and their families evacuated from the Burmese border to Taiwan in the 1950s and in 1961, who built their own mosque in the 1960s. Poorer, more devout and more Arabic-literate than the Taipei establishment, they seek scholarships for their young men to study in Arab countries.

Shaped by the reformist Yihewani tradition of the Chinese northwest and by Muslim Brotherhood writings arriving from the Arab world, they preach Islamic renewal through education, mosque-based welfare, Arabic schooling and moral life in a modern society. Anti-communist and loyal to the state, they press for religious education and recognition of the Muslim veterans.

13.name: Guoji Jingji Hezuo Fazhan Weiyuanhui
13.english: Council for International Economic Cooperation and Development
13.native_full: Xingzhengyuan Guoji Jingji Hezuo Fazhan Weiyuanhui
13.text:
The Council for International Economic Cooperation and Development, created in 1963 to take over the planning work of the American aid era, is the brain trust of Taiwan's economic take-off. Under Premier Yen Chia-kan, technocrats such as Finance Minister K. T. Li and Communications Minister Sun Yun-suan steer the export drive and the Kaohsiung export processing zone opened in 1966.

Its creed is development first: export-led industrialisation, foreign investment, stable money and infrastructure, with politics left to the party. The technocrats are pro-American and pragmatic, increasingly backed by Vice-Premier Chiang Ching-kuo, and their leverage lies in growth rates near ten per cent that underpin the regime's legitimacy.

14.name: Difang Paixi
14.text:
Taiwan's local factions are the clan-based political machines that dominate county and township elections, farmers' associations and credit cooperatives. In Kaohsiung County the Black Faction of Yu Teng-fa vies with the White and Red factions; Changhua, Taichung and Yunlin have their own dynasties of island-born notables, whom the Kuomintang plays off against each other in exchange for loyalty.

Conservative, local and pragmatic, the factions care less about the mainland than about irrigation, roads, credit and jobs for their followers. They back the Kuomintang when rewarded and drift towards independent candidates when slighted, and their leverage lies in delivering the rural Taiwanese vote and controlling the purse strings of the countryside.

15.name: Zhonghua Minguo Gongshang Xiejinhui
15.english: Chinese National Association of Industry and Commerce
15.text:
The Chinese National Association of Industry and Commerce, founded in 1952, gathers the island's leading industrialists and the old Taiwanese landed families who became businessmen after the land reform, when they were compensated with shares in state enterprises. Its leading figures include Koo Chen-fu of the Koo family conglomerate, while newer tycoons such as Wang Yung-ching of Formosa Plastics are rising beside them.

It speaks for big business: export subsidies, cheap credit, labour discipline under martial law, protection of the home market and close ties to Japanese and American capital. Its leverage lies in finance and in the personal channels its members keep to Chiang Ching-kuo and the economic ministries.

16.name: Ziyou Jingji Pai
16.text:
The Free Economy School is the circle of liberal economists who since the 1950s have urged Taipei to dismantle controls. Its intellectual leaders, the Chinese-American economists S. C. Tsiang and Ta-Chung Liu, advised the government on the foreign-exchange and interest-rate reforms of 1958–60, and their students now staff universities, banks and planning offices.

They want market prices, a unified exchange rate, low tariffs, an independent central bank and the privatisation of state monopolies such as sugar, tobacco and petroleum. Anti-communist and pro-American, they have little popular base but considerable influence through the economics faculties, the business press and their access to the technocrats.

17.name: Zhong-Mei Nongcun Fuxing Lianhe Weiyuanhui
17.english: Sino-American Joint Commission on Rural Reconstruction
17.text:
The Sino-American Joint Commission on Rural Reconstruction, set up in Nanjing in 1948 and moved to Taiwan in 1949, is an American-funded body that planned land reform, farmers' associations and irrigation. Since the death of Chiang Monlin in 1964 it has been chaired by the agronomist Shen Tsung-han, and its experts run soil-and-water conservation, forestry and watershed programmes in the central mountains.

Its outlook is scientific and conservationist: protecting slopes and forests from erosion, managing reservoirs and fisheries, controlling pesticides and keeping the countryside productive as industry spreads. Pro-American and apolitical, it speaks for agronomists, foresters and rural extension workers, and draws its leverage from American funds and its record.

18.name: Taiwan Duli Jianguo Lianmeng
18.text:
The World United Formosans for Independence is being formed at the turn of 1970, uniting the United Formosans for Independence in America, the Taiwan Youth Independence League in Japan and groups in Canada and Europe. Its organisers include George Chang (Chang Tsan-hung) in the United States and Ng Chiau-tong in Tokyo, while the jurist Peng Ming-min, under surveillance in Taipei, is the symbol of their cause.

It demands a sovereign Republic of Taiwan, an end to the mainlander-dominated regime and martial law, self-determination for the island-born majority and progressive social reforms. It seeks American support against Beijing's claims, and its leverage lies among Taiwanese students abroad and in the island's resentment of mainlander rule.

19.name: Minzhu Taiwan Lianmeng
19.text:
The Democratic Taiwan Alliance is a Marxist study circle of young writers and artists around the novelist Chen Ying-chen, broken up by the security services in 1968. Chen and his friends are serving long prison sentences for reading Mao Zedong, Lu Xun and other banned literature, yet their ideas circulate among students through hand-copied texts and literary magazines.

They embrace an independent Marxism inspired by Mao and the Third World: anti-imperialism, critique of American and Japanese economic domination, solidarity with workers and peasants, and a Chinese national identity that rejects both Kuomintang dictatorship and Taiwanese separatism. Their leverage lies in literature, campus reading groups and the prestige of political prisoners.

20.name: Zhongguo Qingniandang
20.text:
Founded in Paris in 1923 by Zeng Qi, Li Huang and other Chinese students, the Young China Party is the oldest of the minor parties of the Republic of China. Since Zeng Qi's death in 1951 it has split into quarrelling factions, but it remains a legal 'friendly party' with seats in the National Assembly and the Legislative Yuan, subsidised by the government. Its co-founder Li Huang is its most prominent elder.

Its creed is statism: the nation above class and party, uncompromising anti-communism, a strong state and the recovery of the mainland, mixed with criticism of Kuomintang corruption and one-party privilege. It appeals to nationalist intellectuals, teachers and mainland veterans.

21.name: Lanyishe
21.text:
The Blue Shirts were the secret elite of Whampoa officers who in the 1930s, as the Society for Vigorous Practice, preached unconditional obedience to Chiang Kai-shek, the militarisation of society and the New Life Movement. Dissolved in 1938, they live on as a network of ageing veterans and their disciples in the security services, party schools and military academies, among them their founder Teng Wen-yi.

They admire discipline, a cult of the leader, corporatist organisation and the ruthless suppression of communists and dissidents, and regard democracy as a luxury for peacetime. Their leverage lies in loyalties forged at Whampoa, in the intelligence services and in the martial-law courts.

22.name: Zhongguo Guomindang
22.text:
The Kuomintang, the Chinese Nationalist Party founded by Sun Yat-sen, has ruled Taiwan as a party-state since retreating from the mainland in 1949. Its Director-General, President Chiang Kai-shek, now 82, governs under martial law and the Temporary Provisions that suspend constitutional limits, while his son Chiang Ching-kuo, appointed vice-premier in 1969, is steadily taking over the levers of power.

It claims to be the legitimate government of all China, holds the Chinese seat at the United Nations and pledges to recover the mainland. Its programme combines Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People with anti-communism, land reform and state-guided capitalism, and it relies on the armed forces, the security services, American protection and a growing middle class.

23.name: Yanshenggong Fu
23.text:
The House of Kong, the lineage of Confucius, is the oldest noble family in China; its head bore the hereditary title Duke Yansheng from 1055 until the Republic converted it into the office of Sacrificial Official to Confucius in 1935. The 77th-generation heir, Kung Te-cheng, followed the government to Taiwan in 1949, teaches at National Taiwan University and presides over the rites at Confucian temples.

It embodies the ideal of hereditary virtue, ritual hierarchy and Confucian kingship that survives among traditionalist scholars and elders. Monarchist sentiment in Taiwan, nostalgic for an ethical sovereign above party politics, gathers around the clan, whose leverage is moral: it is the living symbol of the civilisation Chiang's Cultural Renaissance Movement exalts.
